question: During a tracheostomy, the surgeon makes the tracheal incision at the level of the first tracheal ring. Why is this incorrect, and what complication is most likely to follow?

answers.text: Incision at the first ring risks injury to the cricoid cartilage and the consequent subglottic stenosis.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The cricoid is the only complete cartilaginous ring and provides structural support to the subglottis. A tracheostomy too high (at or above the first ring) risks perichondritis and damage to the cricoid, leading to subglottic stenosis — a serious long-term complication. The correct level is the 2nd-3rd tracheal ring.

answers.text: Incision at the first ring risks entering the cricothyroid space and damaging the vocal cords.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The cricothyroid space is above the cricoid cartilage, not at the first ring. Incision at the first ring risks the cricoid cartilage itself, leading to subglottic stenosis — not direct vocal cord injury.

answers.text: Incision at the first ring risks the innominate artery, which crosses the trachea at this level.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The innominate artery crosses the trachea low (at approximately the 7th ring in adults). A high tracheostomy at the first ring carries the risk of subglottic stenosis via cricoid damage, not innominate artery injury.

answers.text: Incision at the first ring makes tube insertion more difficult because the thyroid isthmus overlies this level.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The thyroid isthmus overlies the 2nd-4th tracheal rings — the standard tracheostomy site — not a reason to avoid the first ring. The first ring is avoided specifically to protect the cricoid and prevent subglottic stenosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: The standard tracheostomy site is the 2nd-3rd tracheal ring. Incision at the first ring damages the cricoid (the only complete cartilaginous ring), causing perichondritis and subglottic stenosis. Review tracheostomy technique.
Correct. Tracheostomy is performed at the 2nd-3rd tracheal ring. The first ring is avoided to protect the cricoid cartilage and prevent subglottic stenosis.
